question: The First Five Year Plan of India (1951-56) was based on which economic growth model?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Harrod-Domar model.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The First Five Year Plan (1951-56) was based on the Harrod-Domar model, which holds that the rate of growth of an economy depends on its rate of saving and investment and on the capital-output ratio. (पहली पंचवर्षीय योजना — हैरोड-डोमर मॉडल)

 

• It was drafted under Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru and presented to Parliament in December 1951.

 

• Its priority was agriculture, including irrigation and power, because the country was still recovering from the disruption of Partition and from food shortages.

 

• The target growth rate was 2.1%; the achieved growth rate was 3.6%, making it one of the few plans to exceed its target.

 

• Major projects launched in this period include the Bhakra-Nangal, Hirakud and Damodar Valley projects.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Planning Commission was set up by an executive resolution on 15 March 1950, with the Prime Minister as ex-officio Chairman. It was replaced by NITI Aayog on 1 January 2015.

 

• India's Five Year Plans ended with the Twelfth Plan (2012-17).

 

NOTE

 

• Mahalanobis model (Option 1): The basis of the Second Five Year Plan (1956-61), which shifted the emphasis to heavy and basic industries. It was formulated by P.C. Mahalanobis, founder of the Indian Statistical Institute.

 

• Bombay Plan model (Option 2): The Bombay Plan (1944) was a proposal by eight leading industrialists, including J.R.D. Tata and G.D. Birla, drafted before Independence. It was not a plan model adopted by the Planning Commission.

 

• Wage-goods model (Option 3): Associated with C.N. Vakil and P.R. Brahmananda, who argued that development should begin by expanding the supply of wage goods (essential consumer goods). It was never adopted as the basis of a plan.

question: Who compiled the "Ain-i-Akbari", the detailed account of the administration of Emperor Akbar?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Abul Fazl.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Abul Fazl was a close companion of Akbar and one of the Navaratnas (nine gems) of his court. He compiled the Ain-i-Akbari. (आइन-ए-अकबरी — अबुल फजल)

 

• The Ain-i-Akbari is the third and final volume of the larger work Akbarnama, the official chronicle of Akbar's reign.

 

• While the first two volumes narrate history, the Ain-i-Akbari is administrative and statistical: it records the organisation of the household, the army and the provinces, along with revenue rates, prices, wages, crops and the customs of the people.

 

• It is therefore the single most important source for the economic and administrative history of Mughal India.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Abul Fazl was killed in 1602 by Bir Singh Bundela, at the instigation of Prince Salim (later Jahangir), who resented his influence over Akbar.

 

• The empire under Akbar was divided into subas (provinces), each under a Subedar, and further into sarkars and parganas.

 

NOTE

 

• Abdul Qadir Badauni (Option 1): Author of the Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh, a history of Akbar's reign written secretly and highly critical of the emperor's religious policy — the counterweight to Abul Fazl's official account.

 

• Faizi (Option 3): The elder brother of Abul Fazl and poet laureate (Malik-ush-Shuara) of Akbar's court. He translated the *Lilavati*, a Sanskrit work on mathematics, into Persian.

 

• Raja Todar Mal (Option 4): Akbar's revenue minister, who devised the Zabti or Dahsala land revenue system, known as Todar Mal's Bandobast. He was an administrator, not a chronicler.

question: The Ahom kingdom of Assam was administered through a compulsory labour-service system known as the _____.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Paik system.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Ahom kingdom of Assam was organised around the Paik system, under which every able-bodied adult male, called a paik, owed the state a fixed period of compulsory labour or military service each year in return for a plot of land. (पाइक प्रथा — अहोम राज्य)

 

• Paiks were grouped into units of four called a got. At any given time one paik from each got was on duty for the state while the remaining three cultivated his land, so that service never left a family's fields untended.

 

• Officials were designated by the number of paiks under them — a Bora commanded 20, a Saikia 100, a Hazarika 1,000, a Rajkhowa 3,000 and a Phukan 6,000.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Ahoms were a Tai people who entered the Brahmaputra valley in 1228 CE under Sukapha, the founder of the kingdom. The state lasted about 600 years, until it was annexed by the British after the Treaty of Yandabo (1826).

 

• The Ahoms famously defeated the Mughals under Lachit Borphukan at the Battle of Saraighat (1671) on the Brahmaputra.

 

• Sukapha Day, or Asom Divas, is observed on 2 December.

 

NOTE

 

• Mansab system (Option 1): The Mughal system of ranking nobles, introduced by Akbar, in which each officer held a zat (personal rank) and a sawar (cavalry rank).

 

• Garh system (Option 2): The administrative units of the Gond kingdom of central India, each garh being held by a local chieftain — the origin of names such as Garha-Katanga.

 

• Khalsa system (Option 3): In Mughal revenue administration, khalsa land was crown land, the revenue of which went directly to the imperial treasury rather than to a jagirdar. The term is not connected with Ahom administration.

question: The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 classified industries into how many categories or schedules?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Three.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Industrial Policy Resolution (IPR) of 1956 divided industries into three schedules — A, B and C. (औद्योगिक नीति प्रस्ताव 1956 — तीन अनुसूचियाँ)

 

• Schedule A — 17 industries reserved exclusively for the State, including arms and ammunition, atomic energy, iron and steel, heavy machinery, air transport and railways.

 

• Schedule B — 12 industries in which the State would progressively take the lead while private enterprise could supplement its effort, such as aluminium, machine tools, fertilisers and road transport.

 

• Schedule C — all remaining industries, left to the private sector, though still subject to licensing.

 

• The IPR 1956 is often called the "Economic Constitution of India", and it gave effect to the goal of a socialistic pattern of society adopted at the Avadi session of the Congress in 1955.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The IPR 1956 was the framework for the Second Five Year Plan (1956-61), which was based on the Mahalanobis model of heavy industry.

 

• The first Industrial Policy Resolution was adopted in 1948. The framework of 1956 governed Indian industry until the New Industrial Policy of 24 July 1991, which abolished industrial licensing for most industries and reduced the reserved public sector list from 17 industries to 8.

 

NOTE

 

• Do not confuse the three schedules of IPR 1956 with the Industrial Policy Statement of 1980, which raised the investment ceiling for tiny units, or with the Industrial Policy Statement of 1977, which emphasised cottage and small-scale industries and introduced the concept of the District Industries Centre.

question: What is the molecular formula of sucrose, the common table sugar?
solution_text:
The correct answer is C12H22O11.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The molecular formula of sucrose is C12H22O11. (सुक्रोज — C12H22O11)

 

• Sucrose is a disaccharide, formed by the joining of one molecule of glucose and one molecule of fructose, with the loss of one molecule of water.

 

• This is why the formula is not simply double that of glucose:

 

• Glucose C6H12O6 + Fructose C6H12O6 = C12H24O12

 

• Minus one water molecule (H2O) = C12H22O11

 

• Sucrose is obtained commercially from sugarcane and sugar beet.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Classification of carbohydrates:

 

• Monosaccharides (single sugar units): glucose, fructose, galactose — all C6H12O6

 

• Disaccharides (two units): sucrose (glucose + fructose), maltose (glucose + glucose), lactose (glucose + galactose) — all C12H22O11

 

• Polysaccharides (many units): starch, cellulose, glycogen — (C6H10O5)n

 

• The enzyme sucrase (invertase) breaks sucrose down into glucose and fructose during digestion.

 

NOTE

 

• C6H12O6 (Option 1): The formula of glucose, and also of fructose and galactose — these three are isomers, having the same formula but different structures.

 

• C6H10O5 (Option 2): The repeating unit of polysaccharides such as starch and cellulose, written as (C6H10O5)n.

 

• C12H24O12 (Option 3): The arithmetical sum of two glucose molecules. It is wrong because the loss of one water molecule during the linkage is not accounted for.

question: Which chamber of the human heart pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta for distribution to the body?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Left ventricle.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The left ventricle receives oxygenated blood from the left atrium and pumps it into the aorta, the largest artery of the body, from which it is distributed to all the tissues. (बायाँ निलय — महाधमनी)

 

• The left ventricle has the thickest muscular wall of the four chambers, because it must generate enough pressure to drive blood through the entire systemic circulation.

 

• The valve between the left ventricle and the aorta is the aortic valve, which prevents the backflow of blood into the ventricle.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The path of blood through the heart:

 

• Right atrium ← deoxygenated blood from the body, via the vena cava

 

• Right ventricle → to the lungs, via the pulmonary artery

 

• Left atrium ← oxygenated blood from the lungs, via the pulmonary veins

 

• Left ventricle → to the body, via the aorta

 

• The pulmonary artery is the only artery carrying deoxygenated blood, and the pulmonary vein the only vein carrying oxygenated blood.

 

• The valve between the left atrium and left ventricle is the bicuspid or mitral valve; between the right atrium and right ventricle, the tricuspid valve.

 

NOTE

 

• Right atrium (Option 1): Receives deoxygenated blood returning from the body. Atria are receiving chambers, not pumping chambers, and their walls are thin.

 

• Right ventricle (Option 2): Pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs through the pulmonary artery. Its wall is thinner than the left ventricle's because the lungs are close by and require lower pressure.

 

• Left atrium (Option 3): Receives oxygenated blood from the lungs and passes it to the left ventricle. It does not open into the aorta.

question: The Kalinga War, after which Emperor Ashoka renounced war, was fought in approximately which year?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 261 BCE.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Kalinga War was fought in about 261 BCE, in the eighth year of the reign of Ashoka. (कलिंग युद्ध — लगभग 261 ईसा पूर्व)

 

• Kalinga corresponds broadly to modern Odisha and parts of northern Andhra Pradesh.

 

• The war is described by Ashoka himself in Major Rock Edict XIII, which records that 100,000 were slain, 150,000 deported and many times that number perished. It is the only edict in which an ancient ruler expresses remorse for his own conquest.

 

• After the war Ashoka gave up Digvijaya (conquest by arms) for Dhammavijaya (conquest by righteousness), and embraced Buddhism.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Ashoka's edicts were deciphered in 1837 by James Prinsep. In them the emperor calls himself Devanampiya Piyadassi ("Beloved of the Gods, of pleasing appearance").

 

• Rock Edict XIII is notably absent from the edicts found in Odisha itself — in its place stand two Separate Rock Edicts addressed to the officials of the newly conquered province.

 

NOTE

 

• 326 BCE (Option 1): The year of the Battle of Hydaspes, fought between Alexander and Porus on the river Jhelum.

 

• 305 BCE (Option 2): The approximate year of the conflict between Chandragupta Maurya and Seleucus Nicator, settled by a treaty under which Seleucus ceded territory and sent Megasthenes as ambassador.

 

• 185 BCE (Option 4): The year the Mauryan empire ended, when the last ruler Brihadratha was killed by his commander-in-chief Pushyamitra Shunga, founder of the Shunga dynasty.

question:
Which of the following statements regarding Buddhism is/are correct?

I. Vajrayana is also known as the "Vehicle of the Thunderbolt".
II. The Bodhisattva ideal is the central doctrine of the Hinayana school.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only I.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement I is CORRECT. Vajrayana means the "Vehicle of the Thunderbolt" or "Diamond Vehicle", from Sanskrit vajra (thunderbolt/diamond) + yana (vehicle). It arose in eastern India around the 8th century CE and is marked by mantras, rituals and esoteric practice. It spread to Tibet, Bhutan and Mongolia, and is sometimes called Tantric Buddhism. (वज्रयान — वज्र का मार्ग)

 

• Statement II is INCORRECT. The Bodhisattva ideal is the central doctrine of the MAHAYANA school, not of Hinayana.

 

• A Bodhisattva is one who has attained enlightenment but postpones his own nirvana in order to help all other beings attain it. Avalokiteshvara, Manjushri and Maitreya are the best known.

 

• Hinayana ("Lesser Vehicle"), by contrast, holds up the ideal of the Arhat — the individual who attains liberation for himself through his own effort.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The three vehicles at a glance:

 

• Hinayana / Theravada — the older tradition; goal is the Arhat; scriptures in Pali; prevalent in Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand

 

• Mahayana — the later, more liberal school; goal is the Bodhisattva; scriptures in Sanskrit; prevalent in China, Japan, Korea; formally emerged at the Fourth Buddhist Council under Kanishka in Kashmir

 

• Vajrayana — the tantric school; prevalent in Tibet and the Himalayas

 

NOTE

 

• Since Statement I is correct and Statement II is not, Option 2 (Only II), Option 3 (Both I and II) and Option 4 (Neither I nor II) are all ruled out.

 

• The trap here is that Statement II is a true sentence about the wrong school. In statement-based questions, always check the subject of the sentence as carefully as the predicate.

question: "Chapchar Kut", the spring festival of Mizoram, is celebrated in the month of _____.
solution_text:
The correct answer is March.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Chapchar Kut is the most important festival of Mizoram and is celebrated in the month of March. (चापचार कुट — मिजोरम)

 

• It marks the completion of jhum (shifting) cultivation clearing — the period after the bamboo and trees have been cut and left to dry, and before the burning and sowing begin. It is thus a festival of the interval between two hard seasons of agricultural labour.

 

• Its best known feature is the Cheraw, or bamboo dance, in which dancers step between long bamboo staves that are tapped together in rhythm.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Mizoram's other traditional festivals are Mim Kut (celebrated around August-September, in honour of the departed, marked by the offering of the first maize) and Pawl Kut (a harvest festival celebrated in December-January).

 

• Mizoram became a full State on 20 February 1987, the 23rd State of India, following the Mizo Accord of 1986. Its capital is Aizawl.

 

NOTE

 

• January (Option 1): The month of Pawl Kut, the harvest festival, which falls in the December-January period — not of Chapchar Kut.

 

• August (Option 3): Close to the period of Mim Kut, the maize festival, which falls around August-September.

 

• November (Option 4): No major Mizo festival falls in this month. Chapchar Kut is tied to the spring clearing of the jhum fields and cannot fall late in the year.

question: The Calcutta Madrasa, established in 1781 for the study of Muslim law and allied subjects, was founded by _____.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Warren Hastings.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Calcutta Madrasa was established in 1781 by Warren Hastings, the first Governor-General of Bengal, for the study of Muslim law, Arabic and Persian. (कलकत्ता मदरसा 1781 — वारेन हेस्टिंग्स)

 

• Its practical purpose was to train men qualified to assist the courts in the administration of Muslim personal law, since the Company's courts applied Hindu and Muslim law to their respective communities.

 

• It is the oldest institution of higher learning established by the British in India, and survives today as the Aliah University.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The early "Orientalist" phase of British educational policy produced three landmark institutions:

 

• Calcutta Madrasa (1781) — by Warren Hastings, for Islamic studies

 

• Sanskrit College, Benaras (1791) — by Jonathan Duncan, for Hindu learning

 

• Fort William College, Calcutta (1800) — by Lord Wellesley, to train Company servants in Indian languages

 

• This phase ended with Macaulay's Minute (1835) and Lord William Bentinck's decision to promote English education.

 

NOTE

 

• Lord Cornwallis (Option 1): Governor-General from 1786 to 1793, known for the Permanent Settlement of 1793, the separation of revenue and judicial functions, and the Cornwallis Code.

 

• Sir William Jones (Option 3): A judge of the Calcutta Supreme Court who founded the Asiatic Society of Bengal in 1784. He identified the kinship of Sanskrit with Greek and Latin, but he did not found the Madrasa.

 

• Jonathan Duncan (Option 4): The British Resident at Benaras who founded the Sanskrit College at Benaras in 1791 — the parallel institution for Hindu learning, and the standard distractor in this question.

question: The Civil Disobedience Movement was launched with the Dandi March in _____.
solution_text:
The correct answer is March 1930.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Civil Disobedience Movement began with the Dandi March, which Mahatma Gandhi commenced on 12 March 1930 from the Sabarmati Ashram in Ahmedabad. (दांडी मार्च — 12 मार्च 1930)

 

• Gandhi walked about 385 km over 24 days with 78 followers, reaching the coastal village of Dandi on 5 April 1930.

 

• On the morning of 6 April 1930 he broke the salt law by picking up a lump of natural salt, and the movement spread across the country.

 

• The salt law was chosen because the government monopoly on salt touched the poorest household in India, making it the one grievance shared by every class.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The movement was suspended by the Gandhi-Irwin Pact of 5 March 1931, after which Gandhi attended the Second Round Table Conference in London.

 

• In the south, C. Rajagopalachari led a parallel salt march from Tiruchirappalli to Vedaranyam; on the North-West Frontier, Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan led the movement with his Khudai Khidmatgars.

 

NOTE

 

• April 1919 (Option 1): The month of the Jallianwala Bagh massacre (13 April 1919) and of the Rowlatt Satyagraha.

 

• December 1929 (Option 2): The Lahore Session of the Congress, presided over by Jawaharlal Nehru, which adopted the resolution of Purna Swaraj — complete independence. This preceded and prepared the ground for the movement, but the movement itself was launched with the march in March 1930.

 

• August 1942 (Option 4): The month of the Quit India Movement, launched on 8 August 1942 with the call of "Do or Die".

question: "Powada", the folk ballad form that narrates the heroic deeds of warriors and rulers, is traditionally associated with which Indian state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Maharashtra.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Powada (also spelt *Powada* or *Pawada*) is a form of Marathi ballad traditionally sung in Maharashtra, narrating heroic exploits, above all those of Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj. (पोवाडा — महाराष्ट्र)

 

• The performers are called Shahirs, and they sing in a loud, declamatory style accompanied by the daf or dholki, with the audience joining in the refrain.

 

• The earliest known Powada, composed by Agindas, celebrates Shivaji's killing of Afzal Khan in 1659.

 

• During the freedom struggle the form was revived to carry nationalist and, later, social-reform themes.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other folk forms of Maharashtra: Lavani (a lively song-and-dance form performed to the dholki), Tamasha (folk theatre), Bharud, Gondhal and the Dindi and Kala dances.

 

NOTE

 

• Gujarat (Option 1): Known for Garba and Dandiya Raas, and for the folk-song forms Duha and Sugam Sangeet.

 

• Odisha (Option 2): Known for the classical Odissi, and for folk forms such as Chhau (also of Jharkhand and West Bengal), Ghumura and Sambalpuri song.

 

• Karnataka (Option 3): Known for Yakshagana (folk theatre), Dollu Kunitha (drum dance) and Veeragase.

question: What was the theme of World Environment Day 2025, hosted by the Republic of Korea?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Beat Plastic Pollution.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The theme of World Environment Day 2025 was "Beat Plastic Pollution", and the global host was the Republic of Korea, with the main events held on Jeju Island. (विश्व पर्यावरण दिवस 2025 — प्लास्टिक प्रदूषण को हराएं)

 

• World Environment Day is observed every year on 5 June. It is led by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and is the UN's principal vehicle for encouraging awareness and action for the environment.

 

• It was established by the United Nations General Assembly in 1972, following the Stockholm Conference on the Human Environment, and was first held in 1973.

 

• Each year a different country hosts the global celebrations, and a theme is chosen to focus attention on a pressing environmental issue.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• UNEP was established in 1972 and is headquartered at Nairobi, Kenya.

 

• India has hosted World Environment Day twice — in 2011 (theme: *Forests: Nature at Your Service*) and in 2018 (theme: *Beat Plastic Pollution*).

 

• Other environment-related observances: World Ozone Day — 16 September, World Wildlife Day — 3 March, Earth Day — 22 April, World Water Day — 22 March.

 

NOTE

 

• Only One Earth (Option 2): The theme of World Environment Day 2022, hosted by Sweden, marking 50 years of the Stockholm Conference. It was also the slogan of that original 1972 conference.

 

• Ecosystem Restoration (Option 3): The theme of World Environment Day 2021, hosted by Pakistan, which launched the UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration (2021-2030).

 

• Land Restoration and Drought Resilience (Option 4): The theme of World Environment Day 2024, hosted by Saudi Arabia.

question: Which of the following colloids has the dispersed phase as a gas and the dispersing medium as a liquid?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Whipped cream.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Whipped cream is a colloid in which the dispersed phase is a gas (air) and the dispersing medium is a liquid (cream). Such a colloid is called a foam. (फोम — गैस द्रव में परिक्षिप्त)

 

• Whipping forces air into the cream, and the fat and protein in the cream stabilise the tiny air bubbles so that they do not immediately escape — which is why whipped cream holds its shape.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The eight types of colloid:

 

• Solid in liquid — sol (paint, muddy water, ink)

 

• Liquid in liquid — emulsion (milk, butter is the reverse)

 

• Gas in liquid — foam (whipped cream, shaving cream, soap lather)

 

• Solid in gas — aerosol/solid aerosol (smoke, dust)

 

• Liquid in gas — aerosol (fog, mist, cloud)

 

• Solid in solid — solid sol (coloured glass, some alloys, gemstones)

 

• Liquid in solid — gel (jelly, butter, cheese)

 

• Gas in solid — solid foam (pumice stone, foam rubber)

 

• A colloid has particle sizes between about 1 and 1000 nanometres — larger than in a true solution, smaller than in a suspension. It shows the Tyndall effect, the scattering of a beam of light by the dispersed particles.

 

NOTE

 

• Butter (Option 1): A gel — a liquid (water) dispersed in a solid (fat). This is the reverse of milk, which is a liquid-in-liquid emulsion.

 

• Smoke (Option 3): A solid dispersed in a gas — fine carbon particles suspended in air.

 

• Cheese (Option 4): Also a gel — liquid dispersed in a solid, like butter.

question: NISAR, the Earth-observation satellite launched in July 2025, was jointly developed by ISRO along with which space agency?
solution_text:
The correct answer is NASA.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• NISAR stands for NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar, and it is the first joint satellite mission of ISRO and the American space agency NASA. (निसार — नासा-इसरो संयुक्त उपग्रह)

 

• It was launched on 30 July 2025 from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota, aboard the GSLV-F16 rocket.

 

• NISAR is the first satellite to carry two different radar frequencies — an L-band radar provided by NASA and an S-band radar provided by ISRO.

 

• Its purpose is to monitor changes in the Earth's land surface, ice sheets, vegetation and water, scanning almost the entire globe every 12 days. Its data supports the study of earthquakes, landslides, glacier movement, groundwater and crop cover.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• A synthetic aperture radar works by moving a small antenna along the spacecraft's path and combining the returns, so that it behaves like a far larger antenna. Because it uses radar rather than light, it can see through cloud and darkness, by day or by night.

 

• ISRO was established in 1969 and is headquartered at Bengaluru; NASA was established in 1958 and is headquartered at Washington, D.C.

 

NOTE

 

• European Space Agency (Option 1): ESA, headquartered in Paris, works with ISRO on other projects but is not a partner in NISAR.

 

• JAXA (Option 2): The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency. India's collaboration with JAXA concerns the proposed LUPEX lunar polar exploration mission, not NISAR.

 

• Roscosmos (Option 4): The Russian space agency, which assisted India's Gaganyaan programme with astronaut training. It has no role in NISAR.

question: Zaid crops in India are grown in the short season between _____.
solution_text:
The correct answer is March and June.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Zaid crops are grown in the short summer season between March and June, that is, between the harvesting of the Rabi crop and the sowing of the Kharif crop. (जायद फसलें — मार्च से जून)

 

• Because there is little rainfall in this season, Zaid cultivation depends almost entirely on irrigation.

 

• Principal Zaid crops: watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, bitter gourd, other vegetables, and fodder crops.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• India's three cropping seasons:

 

• Kharif — sown with the onset of the monsoon (June-July), harvested September-October. Crops: rice, maize, jowar, bajra, cotton, jute, groundnut, soyabean.

 

• Rabi — sown in winter (October-November), harvested in summer (March-April). Crops: wheat, barley, gram, peas, mustard.

 

• Zaid — the short summer season (March-June).

 

• The word Rabi comes from the Arabic for *spring* and Kharif from the Arabic for *autumn*, each referring to the season of harvest.

 

NOTE

 

• October and December (Option 1): The sowing period of the Rabi crop.

 

• December and February (Option 2): The middle of the Rabi growing season, when the wheat crop is standing in the field.

 

• July and September (Option 4): The Kharif growing season, dependent on the south-west monsoon.

question: In India's Balance of Payments, which of the following is recorded in the capital account?
option_1: Remittances sent home by Indians working abroad
option_2: Earnings from the export of software services
option_4: Receipts from foreign tourists visiting India
solution_text:
The correct answer is External commercial borrowings.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Balance of Payments (BoP) is the record of all economic transactions between the residents of a country and the rest of the world in a given period. It has two main accounts:

 

• The CURRENT ACCOUNT records trade in goods (visibles) and invisibles — that is, services, income and transfers. These transactions do not create a claim or a liability.

 

• The CAPITAL ACCOUNT records transactions in financial assets and liabilities — borrowings, investment and loans. These do create a claim or a liability.

 

• External commercial borrowings (ECBs) are commercial loans raised by Indian firms from lenders abroad. They create a repayment liability, and are therefore a capital account transaction. (बाह्य वाणिज्यिक उधार — पूंजी खाता)

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other items of the capital account: foreign direct investment (FDI), foreign institutional/portfolio investment (FII/FPI), external assistance, banking capital and changes in foreign exchange reserves.

 

• A simple test: ask whether the transaction has to be paid back or gives rise to an ownership claim. If it does, it belongs to the capital account.

 

NOTE

 

• Remittances (Option 1): These are unilateral or unrequited transfers — money sent with nothing given in return. They form part of invisibles in the current account, and India is the world's largest recipient of remittances.

 

• Software service exports (Option 2): Services are the largest component of India's invisibles, and belong to the current account.

 

• Tourism receipts (Option 4): Foreign tourists purchase Indian services — travel, hotels, transport — so these too are services in the current account.

question:
Which of the following statements regarding the central problems of an economy is/are correct?

I. "For whom to produce" concerns the distribution of the national product among the members of society.
II. The central problems arise because resources are scarce and have alternative uses.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both I and II.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement I is CORRECT. The third central problem, "for whom to produce", is the problem of distribution — how the total output of the economy is to be shared among the people who make it up. It is settled largely by the distribution of income and purchasing power.

 

• Statement II is CORRECT. The central problems arise from the twin facts that resources are scarce relative to unlimited human wants, and that those resources have alternative uses. If resources were unlimited, or could be used for only one purpose, no choice would be necessary and no problem would arise. (संसाधनों की दुर्लभता एवं वैकल्पिक उपयोग)

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The three central problems of every economy:

 

• What to produce, and in what quantities — the problem of allocation of resources between goods.

 

• How to produce — the choice of technique, whether labour-intensive or capital-intensive.

 

• For whom to produce — the problem of distribution of the output.

 

• Because every choice means giving up the next best alternative, economics measures cost as opportunity cost — the value of the best alternative foregone.

 

• These choices are represented graphically by the Production Possibility Curve (PPC), which is concave to the origin because of increasing opportunity cost.

 

NOTE

 

• Since both statements are correct, Option 1 (Only I), Option 2 (Only II) and Option 4 (Neither I nor II) are all ruled out.

 

• Note who solves these problems: in a market economy they are settled by the price mechanism; in a centrally planned economy by the government; and in a mixed economy, such as India's, by both together.

question: Which of the following is NOT a method of soil conservation?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Shifting cultivation.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Shifting cultivation is NOT a method of soil conservation. It is a leading cause of soil degradation. (झूम खेती — मृदा क्षरण का कारण)

 

• In shifting cultivation a patch of forest is cleared and burnt, cultivated for two or three years until the soil is exhausted, and then abandoned while the cultivator moves on to a fresh patch.

 

• The practice destroys the forest cover that binds the soil, exposes the surface to rain and wind, and leads to severe erosion and loss of fertility.

 

• It is known by many local names in India — Jhum in the north-east, Podu in Andhra Pradesh and Odisha, Bewar and Dahiya in Madhya Pradesh, and Kumari in Kerala.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Principal methods of soil conservation:

 

• Contour ploughing — ploughing along the contour lines of a slope, so that each furrow checks the flow of water downhill

 

• Terrace farming — cutting steps into a hillside

 

• Strip cropping — alternating strips of crops with strips of grass to break the force of the wind

 

• Shelter belts — rows of trees planted across the direction of the prevailing wind

 

• Afforestation, check dams and crop rotation

 

NOTE

 

• Terrace farming (Option 1): Widely practised in the Himalayan region and in the Western Ghats; the steps reduce the length and steepness of the slope and so slow the runoff.

 

• Shelter belts (Option 2): Rows of trees planted as windbreaks; they have been particularly effective in stabilising the sandy soils of western Rajasthan.

 

• Strip cropping (Option 4): Large fields are divided into strips, with close-growing crops alternating between them to check the wind.

question: Who is the author of the novel "A Suitable Boy"?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Vikram Seth.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "A Suitable Boy" was written by Vikram Seth and published in 1993. (ए सूटेबल बॉय — विक्रम सेठ)

 

• At about 1,350 pages it is one of the longest novels ever published in English in a single volume.

 

• It is set in a newly independent India in the early 1950s, and follows a mother's search for a suitable husband for her daughter Lata, against the background of the first general election and of land reform.

 

• It won the Commonwealth Writers' Prize and was adapted as a BBC television series in 2020. Its sequel, "A Suitable Girl", has long been announced.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Vikram Seth's other works: "The Golden Gate" (1986), a novel written entirely in sonnets; "An Equal Music" (1999); and the travel book "From Heaven Lake", which won the Thomas Cook Travel Book Award.

 

• He was awarded the Padma Shri in 2007 and the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1988 for *The Golden Gate*.

 

NOTE

 

• Amitav Ghosh (Option 1): Author of "The Shadow Lines", "The Calcutta Chromosome", "The Glass Palace" and the Ibis trilogy. He was the first writer in English to win the Jnanpith Award (2018).

 

• Rohinton Mistry (Option 3): Indian-born Canadian novelist, author of "Such a Long Journey", "A Fine Balance" and "Family Matters".

 

• Upamanyu Chatterjee (Option 4): Author of "English, August: An Indian Story", a novel about a young IAS officer posted to a small town.

question: Which was the first Indian state to implement Value Added Tax (VAT), in April 2003?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Haryana.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Haryana was the first Indian state to implement Value Added Tax (VAT), with effect from 1 April 2003. (हरियाणा — वैट लागू करने वाला पहला राज्य)

 

• VAT is a multi-point tax levied at each stage of production and distribution, but only on the value added at that stage. A dealer pays tax on his sales and claims a credit for the tax already paid on his purchases — the input tax credit.

 

• VAT replaced the earlier sales tax, which was a single-point or cascading levy that produced the problem of tax on tax.

 

• Most other states adopted VAT from 1 April 2005.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• VAT was itself subsumed into the Goods and Services Tax (GST), which came into force on 1 July 2017 through the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016.

 

• GST is a destination-based tax on the supply of goods and services, and is administered by the GST Council, chaired by the Union Finance Minister, in which the Centre holds one-third and the States together two-thirds of the votes.

 

NOTE

 

• Maharashtra (Option 1): Adopted VAT along with most other states on 1 April 2005, not in 2003.

 

• Kerala (Option 2): Also adopted VAT in 2005. It should be noted separately that Kerala was the first state to set up a State Planning Board and, much earlier, achieved full literacy in 1991 — but it was not first with VAT.

 

• Gujarat (Option 3): One of the later adopters of VAT, in 2006.

question: Under the Goods and Services Tax introduced in India in 2017, what is the highest of the four main tax slabs?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 28 per cent.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Goods and Services Tax (GST), introduced on 1 July 2017, has four main rate slabs: 5%, 12%, 18% and 28%. The highest of these is 28%. (जीएसटी — सर्वोच्च स्लैब 28 प्रतिशत)

 

• A zero rate (0%) applies to essential items such as fresh vegetables, milk and unbranded food grains.

 

• Special rates apply to a few goods — 0.25% on rough precious stones and 3% on gold.

 

• Over and above the 28% slab, a compensation cess is levied on certain luxury and demerit goods, such as tobacco products, aerated drinks and large motor cars.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The structure of GST:

 

• CGST — levied by the Centre on intra-state supply

 

• SGST — levied by the State on intra-state supply

 

• IGST — levied by the Centre on inter-state supply and imports, and then apportioned

 

• GST was brought in by the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016, which inserted Article 246A and Article 279A (the GST Council).

 

• Items presently outside GST: petroleum crude, petrol, diesel, natural gas, aviation turbine fuel, alcohol for human consumption, and electricity.

 

NOTE

 

• 18 per cent (Option 1): A genuine GST slab, and the one covering the largest number of goods and services — but not the highest.

 

• 24 per cent (Option 2): Not a GST slab at all. No such rate exists in the structure.

 

• 32 per cent (Option 4): Also not a GST slab. The confusion arises because the effective burden on some demerit goods exceeds 28% once the compensation cess is added — but the slab itself remains 28%.

question: The Kailasa temple at Ellora, carved out of a single rock, was built under the patronage of which dynasty?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rashtrakuta.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Kailasa (Kailasanatha) temple at Ellora, Maharashtra was built in the 8th century CE under the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I. (कैलाश मंदिर, एलोरा — राष्ट्रकूट)

 

• It is the largest monolithic rock-cut structure in the world, carved downward from the top of a single basalt hill, so that the sculptors removed an estimated 200,000 tonnes of rock and built without any assembly of stones.

 

• The temple is dedicated to Lord Shiva and is designed to represent Mount Kailasa, his abode.

 

• It is Cave 16 of the Ellora complex, which was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Ellora caves, numbering 34 in all, are remarkable for representing three religions at one site — Buddhist (caves 1-12), Hindu (13-29) and Jain (30-34).

 

• The nearby Ajanta caves, also a UNESCO site, are entirely Buddhist and are famous for their paintings rather than their sculpture.

 

• Rashtrakuta capital: Manyakheta (Malkhed). Notable rulers: Dantidurga (the founder), Krishna I, Govinda III and Amoghavarsha, author of the Kannada work Kavirajamarga.

 

NOTE

 

• Chalukya (Option 1): Builders of the temples at Badami, Aihole and Pattadakal in Karnataka. Aihole is called the "cradle of Indian temple architecture".

 

• Pallava (Option 2): Builders of the Pancha Rathas and the Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram, and of the Kailasanathar temple at Kanchipuram. Note that the Pallavas also built a temple named *Kailasanatha*, which is the intended confusion in this question — but it is at Kanchipuram, not Ellora.

 

• Chola (Option 4): Builders of the Brihadeshwara temple at Thanjavur, constructed by Rajaraja I, and of the temples at Gangaikondacholapuram and Darasuram.

question: The nitrogen-fixing bacteria found in the root nodules of leguminous plants belong to which genus?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rhizobium.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Rhizobium is the genus of bacteria that lives symbiotically in the root nodules of leguminous plants — gram, pea, groundnut, soyabean, beans and other pulses. (राइजोबियम — मूल ग्रंथिकाएँ)

 

• These bacteria fix atmospheric nitrogen (N2), converting it into ammonia and then into nitrogenous compounds that the plant can absorb. In return the plant supplies the bacteria with carbohydrates and shelter — a classic symbiotic relationship.

 

• Because of this, growing a legume enriches the soil with nitrogen instead of depleting it, which is the basis of the age-old practice of crop rotation — a pulse crop alternated with a cereal such as wheat.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The nitrogen cycle in brief:

 

• Nitrogen fixation — atmospheric N2 converted to ammonia, by Rhizobium (symbiotic), Azotobacter and Clostridium (free-living in soil), Anabaena and Nostoc (blue-green algae), and also by lightning

 

• Nitrification — ammonia to nitrite by Nitrosomonas, and nitrite to nitrate by Nitrobacter

 

• Denitrification — nitrate back to free nitrogen, by Pseudomonas

 

• Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the atmosphere, but plants cannot use it in its free gaseous form — which is why fixation matters.

 

NOTE

 

• Nitrosomonas (Option 1): Carries out the first step of nitrification, oxidising ammonia to nitrite. It lives free in the soil, not in root nodules.

 

• Nitrobacter (Option 3): Carries out the second step of nitrification, oxidising nitrite to nitrate. It too is a free-living soil bacterium.

 

• Pseudomonas (Option 4): Responsible for denitrification, returning nitrogen from the soil to the atmosphere — the reverse of what the question asks about.

question: "Pena", a traditional one-stringed instrument played with a bow, is associated with which state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Manipur.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Pena is a traditional one-stringed bowed instrument of Manipur, played by the Meitei community. (पेना — मणिपुर)

 

• It has two parts: the maithak, a hollow resonator made from a dried gourd or coconut shell covered with animal hide, and the cheijing, the bow, whose string is traditionally of horsehair.

 

• The Pena is central to Lai Haraoba, the great ritual festival of Manipur, where the player, called a Pena Khongba, both plays and sings the narratives of creation.
